en: On the tenth morning of his suspense, he was startled by the sun shining into the room, where a heavy sleep had overtaken him when it was still dark.

en: He rubbed his eyes and woke up, but at first he doubted if he was actually awake.

en: Looking into the Doctor’s room, he saw that the shoemaker’s bench and tools were put away, and the Doctor himself sat reading by the window.

raw: He was in his usual morning dress, and his face (which Mr. Lorry could distinctly see), though still very pale, was calmly studious and attentive.
en: He was dressed in his usual morning clothes, and his face, though still very pale, looked calm and focused.

en: Lorry felt uncertain for a few moments whether the shoemaking had been a dream. His friend sat before him in his usual clothes and appearance, working as normal, with no sign that any change had occurred.

en: Lorry said:

raw: “My dear Manette, I am anxious to have your opinion, in confidence, on a very curious case in which I am deeply interested; that is to say, it is very curious to me; perhaps, to your better information it may be less so.”
en: "My dear Manette, I want to ask your confidential opinion on a very strange case in which I am interested. It seems very strange to me, though it might be simple to you."

raw: Glancing at his hands, which were discoloured by his late work, the Doctor looked troubled, and listened attentively.
en: Looking at his hands, which were stained from his late work, the Doctor looked worried and listened closely.

raw: He had already glanced at his hands more than once.
en: He had already looked at his hands several times.

raw: “Doctor Manette,” said Mr.
en: "Doctor Manette," Mr.

raw: Lorry, touching him affectionately on the arm, “the case is the case of a particularly dear friend of mine.
en: Lorry said, touching his arm, "the case concerns a very dear friend of mine.

raw: Pray give your mind to it, and advise me well for his sake--and above all, for his daughter’s--his daughter’s, my dear Manette.”
en: Please advise me for his sake, and especially for his daughter's sake."

raw: “If I understand,” said the Doctor, in a subdued tone, “some mental shock--?”
en: "I understand," the Doctor said quietly. "A mental shock?"

raw: “Yes!”
en: "Yes!"

raw: “Be explicit,” said the Doctor. “Spare no detail.”
en: "Tell me everything," said the Doctor. "Spare no detail."

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry saw that they understood one another, and proceeded.
en: Lorry saw they understood each other, and continued:

raw: “My dear Manette, it is the case of an old and a prolonged shock, of great acuteness and severity to the affections, the feelings, the--the--as you express it--the mind. The mind.
en: "My dear Manette, it is the case of a severe mental shock that affected the sufferer's mind.

raw: It is the case of a shock under which the sufferer was borne down, one cannot say for how long, because I believe he cannot calculate the time himself, and there are no other means of getting at it.
en: It's a case of a shock that overwhelmed the sufferer for an unknown amount of time, because I believe he can't calculate the time himself, and there's no other way to find out.

raw: It is the case of a shock from which the sufferer recovered, by a process that he cannot trace himself--as I once heard him publicly relate in a striking manner.
en: It is a case of a shock from which the sufferer recovered through a process he can't trace himself—just as I once heard him explain publicly in a striking way.

raw: It is the case of a shock from which he has recovered, so completely, as to be a highly intelligent man, capable of close application of mind, and great exertion of body, and of constantly making fresh additions to his stock of knowledge, which was already very large.
en: It's a case of a shock from which he has recovered so completely that he is a highly intelligent man, capable of deep mental focus, great physical effort, and constantly learning new things to add to his already vast knowledge.

raw: But, unfortunately, there has been,” he paused and took a deep breath--“a slight relapse.”
en: But unfortunately, he has had a slight relapse."

raw: The Doctor, in a low voice, asked, “Of how long duration?”
en: In a low voice, the Doctor asked, "How long did it last?"

raw: “Nine days and nights.”
en: "Nine days and nights."

raw: “How did it show itself?
en: Looking at his hands again, he asked, "How did it show itself?

raw: I infer,” glancing at his hands again, “in the resumption of some old pursuit connected with the shock?”
en: I assume by returning to some old work associated with his past suffering?"

raw: “That is the fact.”
en: "Yes, exactly."

raw: “Now, did you ever see him,” asked the Doctor, distinctly and collectedly, though in the same low voice, “engaged in that pursuit originally?”
en: “Now, did you ever see him,” asked the Doctor, speaking clearly and calmly, though in the same low voice, “engaged in that hobby originally?”

raw: “Once.”
en: "Once."

raw: “And when the relapse fell on him, was he in most respects--or in all respects--as he was then?”
en: "And during the relapse, was he in the same state as before?"

raw: “I think in all respects.”
en: "Yes, in every way."

raw: “You spoke of his daughter.
en: "You mentioned his daughter.

raw: Does his daughter know of the relapse?”
en: Does she know about the relapse?"

raw: “No.
en: "No.

raw: It has been kept from her, and I hope will always be kept from her.
en: We have kept it from her, and hope to keep it a secret forever.

raw: It is known only to myself, and to one other who may be trusted.”
en: Only I and one other trusted person know."

raw: The Doctor grasped his hand, and murmured, “That was very kind. That was very thoughtful!” Mr.

en: Lorry squeezed his hand in return, and they sat in silence.

en: "Now, my dear Manette," Mr.

en: Lorry said gently, "I am only a businessman, and I don't understand these difficult matters.

raw: I do not possess the kind of information necessary; I do not possess the kind of intelligence; I want guiding.
en: I need guidance, and there is no one I trust more than you.

raw: There is no man in this world on whom I could so rely for right guidance, as on you.
en: There is no one in this world I could rely on more for the right guidance than you.

raw: Tell me, how does this relapse come about? Is there danger of another?
en: Is there a danger of it happening again?

raw: Could a repetition of it be prevented?
en: Can we prevent it?

raw: How should a repetition of it be treated?
en: How should we treat it?

raw: How does it come about at all? What can I do for my friend?
en: What can I do for my friend?

en: No man could ever want to help a friend more than I want to help mine, if only I knew how. “But I don't know where to start in a situation like this.

raw: If your sagacity, knowledge, and experience, could put me on the right track, I might be able to do so much; unenlightened and undirected, I can do so little.
en: If your knowledge and experience can guide me, I can do a lot; without guidance, I can do very little.

raw: Pray discuss it with me; pray enable me to see it a little more clearly, and teach me how to be a little more useful.”
en: Please discuss it with me; please help me see it a bit more clearly, and teach me how to be a little more useful.”

raw: Doctor Manette sat meditating after these earnest words were spoken, and Mr. Lorry did not press him.
en: Doctor Manette sat deep in thought after hearing these sincere words, and Mr. Lorry didn't pressure him.

raw: “I think it probable,” said the Doctor, breaking silence with an effort, “that the relapse you have described, my dear friend, was not quite unforeseen by its subject.” “Was it dreaded by him?” Mr. Lorry ventured to ask.
en: "I think it is likely," the Doctor said, breaking the silence with an effort, "that the relapse was not entirely unexpected by the patient."

raw: “Very much.” He said it with an involuntary shudder.
en: "Was he afraid of it?" Mr. Lorry asked.

raw: “You have no idea how such an apprehension weighs on the sufferer’s mind, and how difficult--how almost impossible--it is, for him to force himself to utter a word upon the topic that oppresses him.”
en: "Very much," the Doctor said with a shudder. "You cannot imagine how that fear weighs on a person, and how hard it is for him to speak of it."

raw: “Would he,” asked Mr.
en: "Would it help him," Mr.

raw: But it is, as I have told you, next to impossible.

en: In some cases, completely impossible."

raw: “Now,” said Mr.

en: Lorry said, laying his hand on the Doctor’s arm, "what caused this attack?"

en: Since he recovered so quickly, I would have great hope.

raw: After what has happened, and after his recovery, I find it difficult to imagine any such violent sounding of that string again.
en: After what happened, and after his recovery, I find it hard to imagine anything striking that chord so violently again.

raw: I trust, and I almost believe, that the circumstances likely to renew it are exhausted.”
en: I believe the circumstances likely to cause it are gone."

raw: He spoke with the diffidence of a man who knew how slight a thing would overset the delicate organisation of the mind, and yet with the confidence of a man who had slowly won his assurance out of personal endurance and distress.
en: He spoke with the caution of a doctor who knew how delicate the mind is, but also with the confidence of a man who had survived it himself.

raw: It was not for his friend to abate that confidence.

en: Doctor Manette said after an uneasy pause, "You see, it is very hard to explain the inner workings of this man’s mind.

raw: He once yearned so frightfully for that occupation, and it was so welcome when it came; no doubt it relieved his pain so much, by substituting the perplexity of the fingers for the perplexity of the brain, and by substituting, as he became more practised, the ingenuity of the hands, for the ingenuity of the mental torture; that he has never been able to bear the thought of putting it quite out of his reach.
en: He once longed for that work so much, and it helped relieve his mental pain by keeping his hands busy. Because it helped him survive his mental torture, he could never bear to put it out of reach.

raw: Even now, when I believe he is more hopeful of himself than he has ever been, and even speaks of himself with a kind of confidence, the idea that he might need that old employment, and not find it, gives him a sudden sense of terror, like that which one may fancy strikes to the heart of a lost child.”
en: Even now, when I believe he is more hopeful about himself than he has ever been, and even speaks with a kind of confidence, the thought that he might need that old work and not be able to find it gives him a sudden sense of terror, much like the fear that might strike the heart of a lost child.”
